cards.front: Classify triangles by their sides. Give one example of each.
cards.back: Scalene: all three sides are different lengths (e.g., sides 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm). All angles are also different. Isosceles: exactly two sides are equal (e.g., sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm). The angles opposite the equal sides (base angles) are equal. Equilateral: all three sides are equal (e.g., 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm). All three angles are equal = 60° each.
cards.memory_hook: S-I-E by number of equal sides: Scalene=0 equal, Isosceles=2 equal, Equilateral=all 3 equal. Zero-Two-Three. ZTE.

cards.front: Classify triangles by their angles. What is special about a right-angled triangle?
cards.back: Acute-angled: all three angles < 90°. Right-angled: exactly one angle = 90°. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse (the longest side). Obtuse-angled: exactly one angle > 90° (between 90° and 180°). A triangle CANNOT have two right angles or two obtuse angles (angle sum must be exactly 180°).
cards.memory_hook: ARO = Acute (all sharp/small), Right (one square corner), Obtuse (one large). Right triangle → hypotenuse opposite the 90° angle = longest side. Only ONE of each possible.

cards.front: What is a median of a triangle? What is the centroid?
cards.back: A median is a line segment from a vertex of a triangle to the MIDPOINT of the opposite side. Every triangle has exactly 3 medians. Key property: All three medians of a triangle intersect at a single point called the centroid. The centroid is the 'centre of gravity' or balance point of the triangle — if you balance a triangular card at the centroid, it will not tip over.
cards.memory_hook: MEDIAN = goes to Middle (midpoint). 3 medians → meet at CENTROID (Centre of gravity). M for Midpoint + M for Meet at centroid.

cards.front: What is an altitude of a triangle? What is the orthocentre?
cards.back: An altitude is the perpendicular line segment from a vertex of a triangle to the opposite side (or to the extension of the opposite side in obtuse triangles). Every triangle has exactly 3 altitudes. Key property: All three altitudes intersect at a single point called the orthocentre. In a right-angled triangle, the two legs (sides forming the right angle) ARE the altitudes for each other.
cards.memory_hook: ALTITUDE = Always perpendicular (90°). A for Altitude = A for Angle-90°. 3 altitudes meet at ORTHOCENTRE. In a right triangle, the legs are their own altitudes.

cards.front: State the angle sum property of a triangle. How can it be verified experimentally?
cards.back: Angle sum property: The sum of all three interior angles of ANY triangle = 180°. ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°. Experimental verification: Draw a triangle on paper. Tear off the three corners (vertices). Arrange the three torn angles with their vertices meeting at a point — they always form a straight line (180°). This works for any triangle regardless of its shape or size.
cards.memory_hook: Three angles, ONE rule: always 180°. Like three pieces of a 180° pie. Tear the corners → straight line → 180°. Works for EVERY triangle, no exceptions.

cards.front: Two angles of a triangle are 56° and 79°. Find the third angle. What type of triangle is it?
cards.back: Third angle = 180° − (56° + 79°) = 180° − 135° = 45°. All three angles: 56°, 79°, 45° — all less than 90° → it is an ACUTE-ANGLED triangle. Also, all angles are different → by angles it's acute; by sides it's likely scalene (since all angles different → all sides different).
cards.memory_hook: Missing angle = 180 minus sum of the two known. Check type: all <90° → acute; one =90° → right; one >90° → obtuse.

cards.front: State the exterior angle property of a triangle.
cards.back: An exterior angle of a triangle is formed when one side is extended beyond a vertex. Exterior angle property: An exterior angle of a triangle = the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles (called remote interior angles or opposite interior angles). If the exterior angle is at C, then: Exterior angle at C = ∠A + ∠B. Corollary: An exterior angle is always greater than either of the two non-adjacent interior angles.
cards.memory_hook: EXTERIOR = collects the two FAR/remote angles. Outside angle = sum of the two angles it's 'looking at' across the triangle. EXT = sum of the Excluded Two interior angles.

cards.front: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 52° and ∠B = 68°. Side BC is extended to D. Find the exterior angle ∠ACD.
cards.back: Exterior angle property: ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B = 52° + 68° = 120°. Verification: ∠ACB = 180° − (52° + 68°) = 60°. ∠ACD + ∠ACB = 120° + 60° = 180° ✓ (linear pair on line BD). So ∠ACD = 120°.
cards.memory_hook: Exterior angle = sum of the two angles NOT at C. Add the two 'far' angles. Then verify: exterior + adjacent interior = 180° (linear pair).

cards.front: State the Pythagorean theorem. What is a Pythagorean triplet?
cards.back: Pythagorean theorem: In a right-angled triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c (opposite the right angle): c² = a² + b². Pythagorean triplet: a set of three positive integers (a, b, c) satisfying c² = a² + b². Common triplets: (3, 4, 5): 9+16=25 ✓. (5, 12, 13): 25+144=169 ✓. (8, 15, 17): 64+225=289 ✓. (7, 24, 25): 49+576=625 ✓. Any multiple of a triplet also works: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), etc.
cards.memory_hook: c² = a² + b². Hypotenuse SQUARED = sum of SQUARES of the other two. (3,4,5) is the queen of triplets — memorise it first, then 5-12-13, 8-15-17.

cards.front: Find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs 5 cm and 12 cm.
cards.back: c² = a² + b² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169. c = √169 = 13 cm. The hypotenuse is 13 cm. Recognition: (5, 12, 13) is a standard Pythagorean triplet! Memorising triplets saves time.
cards.memory_hook: 5-12-13: five-twelve-thirteen. 25+144=169=13². One of the four must-know triplets. Recognise the pattern instead of calculating every time.

cards.front: Can 6 cm, 8 cm, and 11 cm be the sides of a triangle? Apply the triangle inequality.
cards.back: Triangle inequality: sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side. Check all three: 6 + 8 = 14 > 11 ✓. 6 + 11 = 17 > 8 ✓. 8 + 11 = 19 > 6 ✓. All three conditions satisfied → YES, these can form a triangle. Quick method: add the two SMALLEST (6+8=14) and check > largest (11). 14 > 11 ✓ → triangle possible.
cards.memory_hook: Quick check: add two smallest, compare with largest. If sum > largest → triangle possible. 6+8=14 > 11 → YES. Always verify all three if time permits.

cards.front: Can 3 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm form a triangle?
cards.back: Check the critical condition: sum of two smallest > largest. 3 + 4 = 7. Is 7 > 8? NO. 7 < 8 → the triangle inequality is NOT satisfied. These three lengths CANNOT form a triangle. Geometric reason: the two shorter sides (3 and 4) are not long enough to 'reach' each other over the base of 8 cm.
cards.memory_hook: 3+4=7, but 8 > 7 → too long a base. The two short sides can't span the gap. NO triangle possible. If the two small ones can't team up against the big one, no triangle.

cards.front: In a right-angled isosceles triangle, one of the acute angles is 45°. Find all angles and describe the side relationships.
cards.back: Right-angled isosceles triangle: one angle = 90°, and it's isosceles → two equal angles → the other two angles are equal. Two equal angles + 90° = 180°. 2x = 90°. x = 45°. All angles: 45°, 45°, 90°. Side relationships: the two legs (sides adjacent to the right angle) are equal. Hypotenuse = leg × √2 (by Pythagorean theorem: c² = a²+a² = 2a², c = a√2).
cards.memory_hook: 45-45-90 triangle: TWO equal legs, hypotenuse = leg × √2. The 'square diagonal' triangle — cutting a square diagonally gives this triangle.

cards.front: An exterior angle of a triangle is 110°. One of the remote interior angles is 65°. Find the other remote interior angle and the third (adjacent) interior angle.
cards.back: Exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles. 110° = 65° + other remote interior angle. Other remote interior angle = 110° − 65° = 45°. Third (adjacent interior) angle = 180° − 110° = 70° (linear pair with exterior angle). Verification: 65° + 45° + 70° = 180° ✓.
cards.memory_hook: Exterior angle = sum of remote interior angles. Subtract one remote from exterior → other remote. Adjacent interior = 180° − exterior. Two steps, two answers.

cards.front: A ladder 13 m long leans against a wall. Its foot is 5 m from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
cards.back: This is a right-angled triangle: hypotenuse = ladder = 13 m, base = distance from wall = 5 m, height = how far up the wall = ? Using Pythagorean theorem: height² = hypotenuse² − base² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144. Height = √144 = 12 m. Recognition: (5, 12, 13) is a Pythagorean triplet! The ladder reaches 12 m up the wall.
cards.memory_hook: Ladder problem = right triangle. Ladder = hypotenuse. Distance from wall = base. Height = ? Use c²=a²+b² rearranged: a²=c²−b². (5,12,13) triplet appears!

cards.front: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2:3:4. Find all three angles. Classify the triangle.
cards.back: Let angles be 2x, 3x, 4x. Angle sum = 180°. 2x + 3x + 4x = 180°. 9x = 180°. x = 20°. Angles: 2×20°=40°, 3×20°=60°, 4×20°=80°. All angles < 90° → ACUTE-ANGLED triangle. All angles different → SCALENE triangle (all sides different).
cards.memory_hook: Ratio problem: assign x, set sum = 180°, solve. Then classify: all <90° → acute. All different → scalene.

cards.front: What is the difference between a median and an altitude?
cards.back: Median: connects a vertex to the MIDPOINT of the opposite side. Bisects (divides into two equal halves) the opposite side. NOT necessarily perpendicular. 3 medians meet at CENTROID. Altitude: a PERPENDICULAR from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension). Creates a 90° angle with the opposite side. NOT necessarily at the midpoint. 3 altitudes meet at ORTHOCENTRE. In equilateral triangles: the median and altitude from each vertex are the SAME line segment.
cards.memory_hook: MEDIAN = Middle-splitter (bisects the side). ALTITUDE = Angle-90° (always perpendicular). In equilateral triangle: they coincide. Otherwise: different lines.

cards.front: Is a triangle with sides 9, 40, 41 a right-angled triangle? Which side is the hypotenuse?
cards.back: Check Pythagorean theorem with c = 41 (largest side = potential hypotenuse): a² + b² = 9² + 40² = 81 + 1600 = 1681. c² = 41² = 1681. Since a² + b² = c² ✓ → YES, it is a right-angled triangle. The hypotenuse is 41 cm (the largest side). (9, 40, 41) is a Pythagorean triplet.
cards.memory_hook: To check if right-angled: square all sides, check if two smaller squares sum = largest square. Always identify the LARGEST side as potential hypotenuse first.

cards.front: Karnataka's BBMP measures a triangular plot with sides 7m, 24m, and 25m. Is the corner at the right angle a true 90°? Which side is opposite it?
cards.back: Check: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². YES — (7, 24, 25) is a Pythagorean triplet → right-angled triangle. The right angle (90°) is the angle between the sides of 7m and 24m. The side of 25m (the hypotenuse) is opposite the right angle. This confirms the plot has a true 90° corner, which is important for land registration and construction layout.
cards.memory_hook: (7, 24, 25): 49+576=625=25². Karnataka land surveyor's check: Pythagorean triplet = right angle confirmed. The hypotenuse is always the LONGEST side.

cards.front: In which type of triangle can altitudes fall OUTSIDE the triangle? Where does the orthocentre lie in each triangle type?
cards.back: Orthocentre location: Acute-angled triangle: orthocentre lies INSIDE the triangle. Right-angled triangle: orthocentre lies AT the vertex of the right angle (the two legs are the altitudes for each other, meeting at the right angle vertex). Obtuse-angled triangle: orthocentre lies OUTSIDE the triangle (since the altitudes must be extended beyond the triangle to meet). This is why in obtuse triangles, altitudes are drawn to EXTENSIONS of the opposite sides.
cards.memory_hook: ORTHOCENTRE location: Acute → INside. Right → AT the right angle vertex. Obtuse → OUTside. AIO / ARO: Acute-In, Right-At, Obtuse-Out.
